studyMetadata.title: STOP&SCAN Expert Panel
studyMetadata.description: Review how STOP&SCAN is used in four real cases and compare it with SIFT and detection and provenance tools.

uiConfig.studyEndMsg: Thank you for completing the STOP&SCAN expert panel. You may close this window.

consent.instruction: Please read the consent document, then confirm the statements in the sidebar.

response.prompt: I have read this document and have had the chance to ask questions.
I understand that participation is voluntary, that I may skip any question, and that I may stop at any time without giving a reason.
I understand that my responses will be recorded under a code, that interaction timestamps within the study page will be logged, and that de-identified quotations may be published.
I understand that once I submit a response within the study I will not be able to edit it.
I am 18 years of age or older.
(Participants in the EEA, UK, or Switzerland) I explicitly consent to my data being processed as described and transferred to the United States.
I consent to take part in this study.

ratings-stopscan.instruction: Rate STOP&SCAN on the items in the sidebar.

response.prompt: Interaction log
A non-expert could follow STOP&SCAN without assistance.
Why? (optional)
The framework includes the right steps and does not leave out anything essential.
Why? (optional)
It is useful to distinguish between the number of steps completed and the number of independent sources of evidence found.
Why? (optional)
Requiring two independent channels before reaching a firm conclusion is an appropriate threshold.
Why? (optional)
A non-expert could tell whether two sources of evidence are genuinely independent.
Why? (optional)
A non-expert could understand that conflicting results from the same type of tool are inconclusive.
Why? (optional)
"Withhold judgment" is a realistic option that people would be willing to accept.
Why? (optional)
STOP&SCAN handles authentic content wrongly described as fake as well as it handles fabricated content.
Why? (optional)

ratings-sift.instruction: Rate SIFT on the items in the sidebar (before our stated critiques).

response.prompt: Interaction log
SIFT remains useful for evaluating content that may be AI-generated or manipulated.
Why? (optional)
Allowing someone to stop after one SIFT move is appropriate.
Why? (optional)
Looking beyond the original webpage or post usually improves a person’s judgment.
Why? (optional)
SIFT provides enough guidance when a trustworthy source publishes incorrect or fabricated content.
Why? (optional)
SIFT provides enough guidance when authentic content is wrongly described as AI-generated.
Why? (optional)
SIFT’s newer guidance adequately addresses content that may itself have been generated by AI.
Why? (optional)

ratings-open.instruction: Optional open critique before we state our positions on SIFT.

response.prompt: Interaction log
Where is STOP&SCAN most likely to fail in everyday use?
Which STOP&SCAN step is weakest? How would you change it?
STOP&SCAN asks people to visit every step, even when an earlier step seems to provide an answer. Is that the right approach?
What, if anything, does STOP&SCAN add that SIFT or lateral reading does not already provide?
What evidence would you need before recommending STOP&SCAN to non-experts?
Is there an approach from your own work that neither framework captures?
Did our examples represent STOP&SCAN fairly, or did they make it look better or worse than it is?

ratings-critique.instruction: Read our positions in the main pane, then respond.

response.prompt: Interaction log
**Q1 — On Stop.** Your response:
Why? (optional)
**Q1 — On Investigate the source.** Your response:
Why? (optional)
**Q1 — On Find better coverage.** Your response:
Why? (optional)
**Q1 — On Trace to the original context.** Your response:
Why? (optional)
**Q2.** Is our concern about SIFT’s AI-specific guidance fair?
Why? (optional)
**Q3.** What concerns or weaknesses in SIFT have we missed?
**Q4.** Which of these concerns do you think is mistaken, and why?
